section.title: Publishing documentation with Markdown::Publish
section.para: This module lets you publish documentation - either in Docbook XML or Markdown format as a static site using publishing engines such as MkDocs etc. You can preview the output before pushing the finished site to GitHub Pages or another static hosting location.

The module assembles the documents and hands them to a publishing engine: MkDocs, VitePress, Docusaurus, or Astro Starlight. Its companion module, ASPEER::MakeMaker::Markdown::Publish, adds make targets to a Perl distribution Makefile. The assembly and publication stage satys in Markdown::Publish, so the same setup can be driven by MakeMaker, a JSON project file, the command-line utility, or Perl code.
The rest of this article explains what those commands do, how source discovery works, how to customise each engine, and how to publish without accidentally mixing local builds with remote operations.

section.title: Quick start
section.para: For quick start configure the MakeMaker adapter, run make doc, then run make publish_serve.

section.title: Workflow
section.para: It helps to separate documentation maintenance from site assembly and publication. They are related, but they do not have the same side effects.

listitem.para: make doc, supplied by ASPEER::MakeMaker::Markdown::Pod, converts maintained DocBook articles to Markdown and merges Markdown sidecars into Perl sources as POD documentation.
A build or preview directs Markdown::Publish to copy the selected Markdown and assets into a temporary assembly, create navigation, and invoke the chosen site generator.
A publication action pushes the completed site somewhere else. GitHub publication updates the "gh-pages" branch; Cloudflare publication invokes Wrangler to push as a Pages site.

note.para: The publisher step expects Markdown. DocBook is an authoring format in the wider toolchain, bit is not understood directly by the site backends. Run make doc after changing an XML article so that its sibling Markdown is current before building the site.

section.title: Documentation layout
section.para: The default convention is to put project articles and explanatory Markdown beneath doc/. Put a module's sidecar Markdown beside the module, such as lib/Example/Client.pm.md, and put an executable's sidecar beside the executable under bin/.
section.programlisting: Example-Client/ ├── Makefile.PL ├── doc/ │ ├── example-client.xml │ ├── example-client.md │ └── images/ │ └── request-flow.svg ├── lib/ │ └── Example/ │ ├── Client.pm │ └── Client.pm.md └── bin/ ├── example-client └── example-client.md
section.para: If there is no doc/, the publisher falls back to the sidecars beneath lib/ and bin/ and will. An explicit sources list replaces these conventions; it is exact rather than additive. Source files and directories named as sources must exist.

A top-level article containing several level-one Markdown headings is split into sections, one per heading. Links to anchors that move into another page are repaired during assembly. If no index.md exists, then the first top-level page also becomes the home page while its original URL remains available.

You can link to markdown documentation for modules and scripts using the convention lib/Examples/Client.pm.md - markdown sidecars will be assembled until the doc/ as a root directory when publishing (i.e. You don't need to specify the document as ../)

section.title: MakeMaker targets
section.para: Options to customise the output can be added to Makefile.PL in META_MERGE.x_documentation.publish section, e.g.
Publisher settings and preferences can also be set with environment variables (see section below).
Regenerate the Makefile after changing Makefile.PL as changing an inline setting also requires regeneration.
section.screen: perl Makefile.PL make doc make publish_serve
section.para: When name is omitted, the MakeMaker adapter uses the distribution's NAME as the documentation title. MkDocs is the default engine, so both module and name can be omitted in this example. Keeping them visible is useful in a template because it makes the intended site clear.

section.title: Work with the make targets
section.para: Once the Makefile has been generated, the adapter supplies targets you can build to.

listitem.para: Assemble the documents and render the static site into the configured output directory, site/ by default.
Assemble the documents and run the selected engine's foreground development server. Stop it with Ctrl-C.
Build the site and create or update the local publication branch, normally gh-pages. It does not contact a remote.
Perform the same local branch update and then push only that branch to origin. The push is not forced but if no clashes will be propagated immediately.
Build the site and deploy its static files with an explicitly configured Wrangler file. It does not update a Git branch.

section.para: The targets call the same engine API as the standalone utility. The MakeMaker adapter does not maintain another implementation of site assembly or Git publication.

section.title: Choose the common options
section.para: Engine settings are flat values in the publish object. They are not nested beneath the selected engine name. These options are shared by the normal workflows:

listitem.para: Selects mkdocs, vitepress, docusaurus, starlight, or a fully qualified installed subclass. MkDocs is the default. You can also supply your own custom module if inheriting, e.g. "ACME::Publish"
An array of source directories. Omit it to use the doc/ convention and sidecar fallback.
The generated site title. Under MakeMaker it defaults to NAME; standalone use otherwise defaults to Documentation.
The rendered site directory. The default is site/.
The deployment path for generated VitePress, Docusaurus, and Starlight configuration. It begins and ends with a slash, for example /example-client/.
The local Git publication branch. The default is gh-pages.
An authored native engine configuration. It is authoritative where the selected backend documents that behaviour.
A supplemental file that customises generated defaults. It cannot be combined with config.
Override the development server listener where the backend supports it.

section.para: MARKDOWN_PUBLISH_MODULE overrides the configured engine at runtime. This is handy for comparing renderers without editing Makefile.PL or a project file:
section.programlisting: MARKDOWN_PUBLISH_MODULE=starlight make publish_serve MARKDOWN_PUBLISH_MODULE=vitepress make publish_build
section.para: MARKDOWN_PUBLISH_HOST and MARKDOWN_PUBLISH_PORT provide global preview defaults. MARKDOWN_PUBLISH_NPM_VERBOSE=1 shows normal npm installation output for the Node-based publishers.

section.title: Select a publishing engine
section.para: All four engines consume the same Markdown source, but their native tooling and configuration differ.

section.title: MkDocs
section.para: MkDocs is the default and the lightest choice for this workflow. Install MkDocs and the theme or plugins required by your configuration. The backend accepts command, strict, address, and output. Strict builds are enabled by default.

A root mkdocs.yml is used directly. Another file named by config is normally inherited by a temporary configuration which supplies the assembled docs_dir, output directory, and navigation. Set config_mode to direct only when the authored file deliberately owns those paths as well.

section.title: VitePress
section.para: VitePress runs in a temporary npm project. Set npm to another npm executable, version to a particular VitePress version, and host, port, or output as needed. An authored configuration named by config keeps its original location so its relative imports still work.

section.title: Docusaurus
section.para: Docusaurus also runs in a temporary npm project and accepts npm, version, host, port, and output. The generated project uses the classic preset, disables the blog, and places the documents at the site root.

section.title: Astro Starlight
section.para: Starlight accepts npm, astro_version, starlight_version, host, port, and output. The generated project includes a Markdown link resolver so links to mirrored module pages become the routes that Starlight actually emits. An authored Astro configuration is wrapped to retain this resolver; if it supplies a Markdown processor, that processor must be unified.

section.title: Extend generated configuration
section.para: Most projects want to retain generated paths and navigation while adding a theme choice, search, social links, or validation policy. Use config_extend for that case. Use config when you intend to own the native engine configuration instead. Supplying both is an error.

section.title: MkDocs supplemental YAML
section.para: MkDocs inherits the named YAML before the publisher supplies its assembly paths and navigation.
section.programlisting: theme: name: material features: - navigation.sections markdown_extensions: - admonition

section.title: VitePress extension function
section.para: VitePress loads an ECMAScript module. Its default export receives the generated VitePress configuration and a context object.

section.title: Docusaurus extension function
section.para: Docusaurus loads a CommonJS module. It returns the complete configuration to use.

section.title: Starlight extension function
section.para: Starlight separates Astro configuration from the options passed to the Starlight integration. Return both objects. Extra Astro integrations are retained after the generated Starlight integration.

section.title: Publish to GitHub Pages
section.para: Start with the local-only action. It builds the site in a temporary directory, creates a temporary Git worktree, replaces the content of the publication branch, commits changed output, and removes the worktree. Your current checkout stays on its existing branch.
section.programlisting: make doc make publish_build make publish_gh git log --oneline --decorate -1 gh-pages git push origin gh-pages
section.para: The final push is shown separately so you can inspect the result first. When that separation is unnecessary, use make publish_gh-push. It updates the same local branch and runs git push origin gh-pages; it does not force the update or push another branch.

GitHub project sites normally live beneath the repository name. During a GitHub publication action, the publisher derives /repository-name/ from origin. A repository named owner.github.io uses /. If no origin URL is available, the checkout directory name is the fallback. Set base explicitly when the published URL uses another path.

warning.para: publish_gh-push will push to remote. Use publish_gh when the repository's authoritative remote is not GitHub, when GitHub is only a mirror, or when you want to review the publication commit before pushing it.

section.title: Use a project.json file
section.para: A standalone project file can be used outside MakeMaker, or inside it when you want publication settings to change without regenerating the Makefile. The conventional filename is doc/project.json. The file may contain the publisher settings directly, beneath publish, or in the complete x_documentation.publish shape used by MakeMaker.
Run the utility from the project root. It automatically reads doc/project.json when present, or accepts another path with --config.
section.programlisting:
markdown-publish build markdown-publish serve markdown-publish gh markdown-publish gh-push
markdown-publish serve --config config/documentation.json
section.para: To make the MakeMaker targets read the same external file, set only config_file in the metadata. Do not combine it with inline publisher options.

The file is read when a target runs, so editing it does not require perl Makefile.PL. This is often the nicest arrangement for a project that changes themes and publishing details more often than its build metadata.

section.title: Use command-line options for a quick build
section.para: A small project does not need a JSON file. Select the engine and common values directly:

Repeat --source to name several exact source roots. The remaining common options are --branch, --version, and --help. Put native engine options, supplemental configuration, and Cloudflare settings in a JSON file; the command line intentionally exposes only the common quick-start choices.
When a project file is selected explicitly or found automatically, --module cannot replace its engine. Use MARKDOWN_PUBLISH_MODULE for a deliberate runtime engine override.

section.title: Publish static assets with Cloudflare
section.para: Cloudflare publication requires a dedicated Wrangler configuration. Keep the Worker name, compatibility date, routes, and other deployment settings there. The publisher builds once and passes the actual output directory to Wrangler with --assets; it does not rewrite the authored file.
Point the publication configuration at that file. The executable defaults to wrangler; an authored Wrangler environment is optional.
section.programlisting: markdown-publish cloudflare --config doc/project.json # or, with the MakeMaker adapter: make publish_cloudflare

warning.para: This command deploys to Cloudflare. Review the Worker name, account, routes, environment, and current Wrangler login before running it. Keep tokens and other credentials out of project metadata and source control.

section.title: Drive the publisher from Perl
section.para: The MakeMaker and command-line entry points are conveniences. A script can construct the selected backend and dispatch the same actions directly.
To read a project file, call Markdown::Publish->load_config() or pass only config_file to the base constructor.
Backend constructors are also available when the engine is already known. The supported actions are build, serve, gh, gh-push, and cloudflare.

section.title: A practical documentation cycle
section.para: A maintainable workflow keeps authored material, generated Markdown, site output, and remote publication distinct.

listitem.para: Edit DocBook articles, Markdown articles, and source sidecars.
Run make doc and review the generated Markdown and POD changes.
Run make publish_serve and inspect navigation, links, code blocks, images, and the home page.
Run make publish_build so strict or production-only build failures appear before publication.
Commit the authored and durable generated documentation through the project's normal source-control workflow.
Run make publish_gh and inspect the local branch, or run an explicitly authorised remote publication action.

section.para: Site assembly happens in temporary directories, while the rendered output uses site/ by default. Keep generated site output out of the source branch unless the project has a specific reason to track it. The publication branch is the durable Git representation of that output.

section.title: When something does not look right

listitem.para: Set name. MakeMaker normally derives it from NAME, but standalone configurations need their own friendly name.

varlistentry.term: GitHub Pages has missing styles or broken links

listitem.para: Check base. Leave it unset for normal repository-name inference, or set the exact path explicitly when the published URL differs.

varlistentry.term: A module sidecar is missing from navigation

listitem.para: This is expected when doc/ exists. Sidecars are mirrored for links, while top-level project articles form generated navigation. Name lib/ explicitly as a source if those pages should become the primary publication.

varlistentry.term: An XML edit is absent from the site

listitem.para: Run make doc. The publisher reads the sibling Markdown generated from the DocBook source.

varlistentry.term: A custom config loses generated navigation

listitem.para: Use config_extend when you want to supplement generated defaults. A config file is intentionally authoritative.
Check MARKDOWN_PUBLISH_MODULE first because it overrides metadata and JSON configuration. Then check the module value in the active configuration source.

varlistentry.term: An npm installation fails without enough detail

listitem.para: Set MARKDOWN_PUBLISH_NPM_VERBOSE=1 and repeat the build to see normal npm output.

section.title: Where to go next
section.para: Start with MkDocs and convention-based discovery. Add explicit sources only when the default boundary is not the one you want. Add a supplemental configuration when the generated site needs a theme or integration. Move to an authoritative native configuration only when the project genuinely needs to own the engine's complete layout.

The module reference for Markdown::Publish describes its methods and publication contracts. The backend module references document engine-specific settings, and ASPEER::MakeMaker::Markdown::Publish documents the MakeMaker adapter. Use those references for exact API details; use this article as the end-to-end map of how the pieces fit together.
